questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: A chant and its unaccompanied unison
questions.learningObjective: state the defining conditions of a plain chant
questions.explanation: The conditions together identify plain chant: one voice at a time so that the texture is monophonic, no instruments of any kind, one note for each syllable so that the text is audible note by note, and a free rhythm derived from the prose of the words instead of a measured pulse. Each of those is doing work. The unison removes any question of harmonic progression, the syllabic setting keeps the text intelligible, and the free rhythm lets a long word be held as long as the sense of the phrase requires. The trap is to read the missing instruments as the only clue, since unaccompanied monophony also describes a single singer and a drum, neither of which carries a liturgical text.
questions.hint: Count the sounding lines and ask what governs the rhythm.

options.text: A plain chant, since one unaccompanied voice, one note per syllable and a word-led rhythm define it
A motet, since a motet is also sacred and is likewise performed without instruments in its earliest form
options.misconception: confuses a polyphonic setting of several words with a monophonic setting of one

options.text: An organum, since the absence of instruments is what forces a second voice to be added above the melody
options.misconception: reads the missing instruments as evidence for added voices rather than for monophony

options.text: A monophonic dance tune, since the free rhythm is what marks a piece as belonging to the dance repertoire
options.misconception: treats a word-led free rhythm as the mark of a dance rather than of a liturgical setting

questions.topic: Doubling a pitch standard up two octaves
questions.learningObjective: compute a frequency two octaves above a stated pitch standard
questions.explanation: Doubling from 435 gives 870 for the first octave, and doubling 870 gives 1740 for the second, so the note two octaves above the reference is 1740 hertz. The second route multiplies by four in one step, since two octaves is two doublings, and 435 times 4 is 1740. The reason a standard is stated as a frequency at all is that this arithmetic is what lets an instrument-maker tune to it: the same number fixes the note, the octave above it and every octave below. The trap is 435, which is the reference note itself rather than anything derived from it.
questions.hint: Double once, then double again, or multiply by four.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Telling a monophonic texture from a polyphonic one
questions.learningObjective: distinguish monophonic from polyphonic texture by sounding lines
questions.explanation: The test is whether the sounding lines can be followed independently. A monophonic texture carries one line at a time, so there is never more than one thing happening and nothing can be traced underneath. A polyphonic texture carries two or more lines at once, each with its own contour, and a listener can follow one while the others continue. Homophony is a third case and does not belong on this scale, because there the lines move together and share a rhythm, which is a texture of chordal support rather than of independent voices. The trap is to confuse polyphony with loudness, so that a big organ sounds polyphonic because it is loud, when a single unaccompanied voice played very loudly is still monophonic.
questions.hint: Ask how many independent lines are sounding and whether they can be followed apart.

options.text: Whether two or more lines sound at once and can each be traced on their own, rather than one line alone
Whether the music is loud or soft, since a quiet single line is monophonic and a loud block of sound is polyphonic
options.misconception: confuses the number of sounding lines with the volume of the sound

options.text: Whether the piece is accompanied or unaccompanied, since instruments are what make a texture polyphonic
options.misconception: believes instruments rather than competing voices create polyphony

options.text: Whether the lines share a rhythm, since a shared rhythm always rules out a polyphonic texture
options.misconception: overlaps homophony with monophony and misses that polyphonic voices may share a pulse

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: A cantus firmus and its role in a polyphonic setting
questions.learningObjective: state what a cantus firmus is and what it contributes to a setting
questions.explanation: That melody is a cantus firmus, a fixed song used as the structural support of a polyphonic setting, and its defining properties are exactly the ones described: it is slow, it is in even long notes, and it is usually taken from an existing chant rather than newly composed. Because it barely moves, it functions as a reference line, so every other voice can be heard in relation to it and the ear always knows where it is. The added voices above supply the movement, the decoration and the harmonic interest. The trap is to think the cantus firmus is the most important voice, when its importance is precisely that it is the least active and the most reliably present.
questions.hint: Ask which voice is not going anywhere, and what the other voices are measured against.

options.text: A cantus firmus, and its stillness makes it the reference line against which the moving voices above are heard
A cantus firmus, and its long note values make it the main melody that the other voices merely accompany
options.misconception: treats the borrowed slow line as the principal tune rather than as the fixed support

options.text: A ground, because a fixed repeating line in the bass is the same device under a different name
options.misconception: confuses a borrowed static melody with a repeating ostinato bass

options.text: A cantus firmus, and its use obliges the voices above to enter one after another rather than to sound together

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The rhythmic device of an isorhythmic section
questions.learningObjective: identify the repeating rhythmic and melodic patterns of an isorhythmic section
questions.explanation: The device is isorhythm, and it works by repeating two things at once that are usually kept separate. The repeating rhythmic pattern is called the color and fixes where the cycles turn over; the repeating melodic pattern is called the talea and fixes what the music plays. Putting them together at different lengths is what produces the section, and the point of choosing a color of 12 and a talea of 4 is that the two cycles fall out of step, so the combination repeats only every three statements of the talea. That staggered result is the whole compositional interest. The trap is to think the two patterns are the same length, which would make the device a plain repetition with no interaction.
questions.hint: Ask what is being repeated at two different levels at once, and name each level.

options.text: Isorhythm, with the repeating rhythm called the color and the repeating melody called the talea
Isorhythm, with the repeating melody called the color and the repeating rhythm called the talea
options.misconception: swaps the two names, which is the standard way to get this backwards

options.text: A ground bass, since both patterns repeat and any repeated pattern in a section is a ground
options.misconception: equates repetition of any kind with a repeating bass specifically

options.text: A sequence, since the same two patterns simply keep restarting at their own lengths
options.misconception: calls two independent cycles a sequence, which requires a transposed repetition

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Counting the cycles in an isorhythmic section
questions.learningObjective: compute how many times a rhythmic pattern repeats before the two cycles realign
questions.explanation: The color lasts 12 units and each statement of the talea lasts 4, so 12 divided by 4 is 3, and the two cycles realign every third statement. The second route counts the statements: the talea begins at units 1, 5 and 9 of the color, and the fourth statement would begin at unit 13, which is one unit past the end of the color, so three is the largest whole number that fits. The reason the composer wants that mismatch is that it stops the section from sounding like a single repeating pattern, since the two cycles only coincide occasionally. The trap is 12, which reports the length of the color rather than the number of times the shorter cycle fits inside it.
questions.hint: Divide the length of the color by the length of the talea.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The text-setting principle of a motet
questions.learningObjective: state how a motet assigns text to its voices
questions.explanation: The device is polytextuality, and it produces what a listener hears as a weave of separate texts sounding at once. Each voice takes a different point in the liturgical text, so the words are staggered, and because the voices then proceed at different rates the alignment breaks down further until each voice is completing its own sense separately. The effect is that the text becomes almost unintelligible as a single narrative and is heard instead as a sound made of words, which is the point of the form. The trap is to assume the voices always sing the same words together, which is the practice of a later setting and not the device that made the motet distinctive.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when several voices sing different words over the same music.

options.text: Polytextuality, which staggers the words across the voices so several parts of the text sound at once
Homophony, which aligns the words across the voices so every part of the text sounds simultaneously
options.misconception: confuses staggered texts with the aligned setting of a single text

options.text: Madrigalian imitation, which requires one voice to copy another's words exactly in turn
options.misconception: borrows the rule of a secular genre and applies it to a sacred form

options.text: A monophonic setting, since the separate words must be taken one after another to be understood at all
options.misconception: believes polytextuality reduces the music to a single line rather than multiplying it

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Telling a madrigal from the other sacred and secular forms
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a madrigal from related genres by its text and its setting
questions.explanation: Form 2 is the madrigal, and the two features that settle it are the vernacular Italian love poetry and the fact that each stanza receives its own text, so the piece runs straight through rather than returning to a refrain. The setting then follows from that: with a fresh text for each stanza, each voice can enter imitatively on the new words, which is what form 2 describes. Form 3 is a courtly song in a fixed form, form 1 is the sacred polyphonic setting, and form 4 is the chant. The trap is to choose form 1 because it is the most elaborate, when a madrigal is defined by what it sets rather than by how many voices it uses.
questions.hint: Ask which row has both a secular vernacular text and a new text for each stanza.

options.text: Form 2, because it sets a vernacular Italian poem and gives each stanza a new text, which is what a madrigal does

options.text: Form 3, because a fixed refrain is the defining feature and the madrigal is simply a long courtly song

options.text: Form 4, because a single unaccompanied line setting a text is the oldest and therefore the defining type

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Distinguishing troubadour from trouvère
questions.learningObjective: state what distinguishes a troubadour song from a trouvère song
questions.explanation: The southern tradition is the troubadour, which writes in the language of the south, and the northern tradition is the trouvère, which writes in the language of the north, so the distinction is one of language, region and repertoire rather than of form or function. Both traditions produce single-voice songs for courtly performance on love, parting and the knightly quest, so a listener hearing a melody alone could not tell them apart; the evidence is in the text and its language. The trap is to treat the two names as a quality judgment, as if the northern songs were a later or weaker version of the southern ones, when they are two independent traditions with their own conventions.
questions.hint: Ask which language each tradition uses and where that language was spoken.

options.text: The troubadour tradition is southern and the trouvère tradition northern, and the two are told apart by their language and repertoire
The troubadour tradition is for solo voice and the trouvère tradition for voices in turn, so the difference is one of scoring
options.misconception: invents a scoring difference where both traditions produce single-voice songs

options.text: The troubadour tradition is sacred and the trouvère tradition secular, so the difference is the subject of the text
options.misconception: makes both traditions sacred, when both are courtly secular song

options.text: The troubadour tradition is earlier and the trouvère tradition is a later copy of it with no distinct repertoire
options.misconception: reduces one tradition to a copy of the other and denies it an identity of its own

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: A courtly genre and its subject
questions.learningObjective: name the principal courtly song genre and the subject it treats
questions.explanation: The genre is the canso, and its subject is the lover's song: a declaration addressed to a lady, usually by a knight, and often cast as a complaint, a request or a farewell rather than as a celebration of an accomplished love. Because the singer is the lover and the address is direct, the genre is where the whole convention of courtly feeling is stated most plainly. The trap is to name the genre by the more technical terms for its musical construction, which describe how the melody is laid out and not what the song is about.
questions.hint: Ask which genre in the repertory is named for what it does rather than for how it is built.

options.text: The canso, which carries the lover's declaration to a lady and is named for that subject rather than for its construction
The virelai, which is named for its repeating refrain and is distinguished by the number of times that refrain returns

questions.topic: Counting the refrains across the formes fixe
questions.learningObjective: add up the refrain counts of the four formes fixe
questions.explanation: Adding the four counts gives 2 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1, which is 8 returns. The second route pairs them: the ballade and the virelai together give 4, the rondeau gives 3, and the estampie gives 1, and 4 plus 3 plus 1 is again 8. The reason a fixed form returns its refrain several times rather than once is that the fixed melody is the frame and the varying upper voices are the substance, so the listener needs the frame to return to hear each new setting as a variation on the same thing. The trap is 4, which is the number of genres rather than the number of returns.
questions.hint: Add the four given counts and watch that the ballade and the virelai are not being counted once each.

questions.topic: Comparing the metres of a basse danse and its saltarello
questions.learningObjective: compare the bar lengths of a basse danse and its saltarello
questions.explanation: A bar of 6/8 contains 6 quavers and a bar of 3/4 contains 3 crotchets, which is 3 times 2, or 6 quavers, so both bars are the same length. That is the point of the pairing, since the saltarello takes the same tune and the same number of steps but moves about twice as fast, and the change of metre is how the notated figures produce that change of speed while the bar length stays fixed. The second route is the same conversion done from the other side: 3/4 gives 3 crotchets and a crotchet is 2 quavers, so 6 again. The trap is 3, which counts crotchets and quavers as the same unit.
questions.hint: Convert each metre into eighth notes and compare the two totals.

options.text: 6 in each, since 6/8 gives 6 quavers and 3/4 gives 3 crotchets which are also 6 quavers
6 in the basse danse and 3 in the saltarello, since the smaller lower number must mean the shorter bar

options.misconception: invents a figure that connects bar length to the number of steps in a dance

options.text: 12 in each, since both dances are in compound metre and compound metres always double the bar

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: What a sign in mensural notation means
questions.learningObjective: state what a note's shape and a following dot mean in mensural notation
questions.explanation: A breve is worth 2 semibreves, and the next smaller note is the semibreve, worth 1, so a dotted breve is worth 2 plus 1, which is 3 semibreves. The second route is the general rule at work: the dot never adds a fixed amount, it adds whatever the next smaller value is, which is why a dotted semibreve is 3 minims while a dotted breve is 3 semibreves. That flexibility is the point of the system, because it lets a composer increase a note by a step without introducing a new shape for the length. The trap is 2, which is the undotted breve, and 4, which is what a dot would add if it were a fixed half rather than the next value down.
questions.hint: Take the note's own value and add the value of the note one size smaller.

options.text: 3 semibreves, since the breve's own 2 semibreves are joined by 1 more, the value of the next smaller note
2 semibreves, since the dot is a decoration and does not change the written value at all
options.misconception: treats the dot as a mark of articulation rather than as an addition of value

options.text: 4 semibreves, since a dot adds half of the note's own value in every system of notation
options.misconception: assumes the dot means the same fixed fraction in all notation systems

options.text: 6 semibreves, since the breve and the semibreve are each written twice over when a dot is added
options.misconception: treats the dot as doubling both notes rather than adding the smaller one

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: What a temperament trades away
questions.learningObjective: state the compromise a temperament makes between intervals
questions.explanation: A temperament spreads error. It exists because the pure ratios of the intervals are mutually inconsistent, so if a composer writes in more than about a third of the octave it is impossible for every fifth and every major third to be pure at once, and a temperament decides which intervals to favour and which to let go out of tune. What every temperament therefore buys is a set of usable keys, and what it costs is accuracy somewhere: in every temperament except equal, some keys are better than others, and in equal temperaments all are equally available and equally slightly wrong. The trap is to think a temperament is a system of tuning mistakes rather than a system of deliberate choices, since the error is the point of the design rather than a failure of it.
questions.hint: Ask what has to give when two intervals are both required to be pure.

options.text: It chooses which intervals to keep pure and which to let go out of tune, since they cannot all be pure at once

options.text: It removes the disagreement between the intervals by redefining them, so that all intervals become pure at once
options.misconception: believes a temperament eliminates the inconsistency rather than distributing it

options.text: It decides which keys are the real keys, so that the other keys were never in tune in the first place
options.misconception: treats a temperament as a discovery about the keyboard rather than a choice about it

questions.topic: Comparing a pure fifth with an equal-tempered fifth
questions.learningObjective: compute the cents difference between a pure and an equal-tempered fifth
questions.explanation: Subtracting 700 from 701.955 leaves 1.955, which rounds to 2 cents. The second route derives both figures instead of trusting them: the cents of a ratio of 3 to 2 is 1200 times the base-2 logarithm of 1.5, which is 1200 times 0.585, giving 701.96, and the equal-tempered fifth is 7 semitones of 100 cents, giving 700, and the difference is the same 1.955. The size of that difference is why the comma between the two fifths is a subject composers can ignore, while the far larger comma between the pure and the equal-tempered major third is not. The trap is 22, which is the size of the comma between two pure fifths rather than the gap between a pure and a tempered one.
questions.hint: Subtract the smaller figure from the larger and round to the nearest cent.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: What quarter-comma meantone compromises
questions.learningObjective: state what quarter-comma meantone gains and what it gives up
questions.explanation: Narrowing the fifths makes the major thirds pure because a major third is built from four fifths less two octaves, and four narrowed fifths cancel most of the narrowing. But a circle of narrowed fifths does not close, so after the usable stretch is exhausted the last fifth has to take up all the accumulated error at once, and that gap is the wolf, which sounds badly out of tune. The result is a compass of roughly half the chromatic octave in which every chord is acceptable, against equal temperament's full compass. The trap is to think the wolf is a defect in the design, when it is the direct consequence of the pure thirds the design is for.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when the fifths are narrowed one after another around a closed circle.

options.text: Narrowed fifths cannot close a circle, so the error accumulates and one interval must take it all, which limits the usable compass

options.misconception: believes the accumulated narrowing vanishes instead of landing on one interval

questions.explanation: A quarter of 21.506 is 5.3765 cents, and subtracting that from 701.955 leaves 696.578, which is 696.58 cents to two decimal places. The result is a fifth about 3.4 cents narrower than the equal-tempered fifth, and twelve such fifths are what fail to come back to the octave, which is the arithmetic behind the wolf. The trap is 701.955, the pure fifth, which is the size the system deliberately gives up.

questions.topic: The size of a major third in meantone

That is the whole bargain of the system, and the price is paid in the fifths rather than in the thirds. questions.explanation: Subtracting 386.312 from 503.422 leaves 117.11 cents, which is 117.1 to the nearest tenth. The second route is by the relation a fourth is a third plus a semitone, so the semitone is the fourth less the third by definition, and the same two figures give the same 117.108. The number matters because it is very far from the 100 cents of an equal-tempered semitone, and a keyboard tuned this way has semitones of noticeably different sizes depending on which letters they fall between. The trap is 100, the equal-tempered figure, which assumes every semitone on the keyboard is the same size.

The consequence is that a meantone keyboard has two quite different semitones, one of them 76 cents and the other 117, and the ear hears that difference as a roughness in the low and middle register. The trap is 100, which would only be right if a meantone keyboard divided the octave into equal semitones like equal temperament does.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The flexibility equal temperament gains
questions.learningObjective: state what equal temperament gains and what it gives up
questions.explanation: It buys the whole keyboard. Because every key is the same distance from every other, a composer can modulate into any of the twelve keys and land in the same one the piece began in, and a player can practise in one key and perform in another without retuning. A meantone keyboard gives purer thirds over part of its compass and refuses the rest, so the composer chooses its key for the sake of the tuning. What equal temperament gives up is accuracy: the major third measures 400 cents against a pure 386, so no triad is quite in tune and the roughness is spread evenly instead of being concentrated in the low register. The trap is to call it the accurate system, when accuracy and availability are being traded against each other.
questions.hint: Ask what a composer can write on a meantone keyboard that cannot be written on an equal-tempered one.

options.text: Every key is equally good, so a composer may modulate anywhere and the roughness is spread evenly rather than piled up
Every interval becomes exact, so a keyboard of this kind is the one that lets a piece be played genuinely in tune
options.misconception: believes equal temperament makes intervals pure rather than merely even

options.text: The fifths stay pure and only the semitones are equalised, so the tuning keeps what the other systems give up

options.text: Nothing, since twelve equal semitones are already what every keyboard provides and so no key is newly gained

Both routes agree, which is worth confirming because 900 is also the size a major third would have in a system that divided the octave differently. The figure matters because it is 16 cents wider than a pure major sixth, and that 16 cents is the price equal temperament charges for making every key available. questions.topic: Transposing a note by a number of semitones
questions.learningObjective: compute the equal-tempered frequency a transposition reaches
questions.explanation: Seven divided by 12 is 0.58333, and 2 to that power is 1.49831, and 440 times 1.49831 is 659.255, which rounds to 659 hertz. The second route is the same computation stated as a ratio of a whole tone: a semitone multiplies the frequency by the twelfth root of 2, which is about 1.05946, and applying that factor seven times to 440 gives the same 659 to the nearest hertz. The reason a multiplication is done rather than an addition is that pitch is a ratio and not a distance, so every interval is a factor and the factors compound. The trap is 550, which adds 110 per semitone and treats frequency as if it were a linear quantity.

questions.topic: The size of a compound interval in equal temperament
questions.learningObjective: compute the cents size of a compound interval in equal temperament
questions.explanation: The fifth is 7 semitones, which is 700 cents, and adding the octave gives 1200 plus 700, which is 1900 cents. The second route is the same addition in semitones and then a conversion: a twelfth is 12 semitones plus 7, which is 19, and 19 semitones at 100 cents each is 1900 cents. The two routes agree, and the point of the figure is that a compound interval is not a different kind of thing, only an ordinary interval displaced by an octave, which is why its size is always the simple interval plus 1200. The trap is 700, which reports the perfect fifth and forgets the octave the twelfth adds to it.

questions.topic: Transposing upward by a fourth in equal temperament
questions.learningObjective: compute the equal-tempered frequency a fourth above a note
questions.explanation: Five divided by 12 is 0.41667, and 2 to that power is 1.33484, and 200 times 1.33484 is 266.97, which rounds to 267 hertz. Both routes agree, and the rounding is safe because 266.97 is well clear of the half hertz. The reason the factor is worth computing is that a fourth is close to but not the same as the simple ratio of four to three, and the gap between 1.3333 and 1.3348 is what equal temperament accepts. The trap is to multiply 200 by 3 divided by 4, which gives 200 and simply returns the starting note.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Musique concrète and its source material
questions.learningObjective: state what musique concrète uses as its raw material
questions.explanation: The practice is musique concrète, and its material is recorded sound taken from the world, which is what the name says: the composer's raw material is concrete sound rather than abstract pitch. Because the sounds arrive already having a pitch, a loudness, an envelope and a location, the resulting music carries all of that with it, and a recording of a door or a train arrives with its own acoustic space inside the piece. The score consequently shows order, duration and level rather than notes, since the sounds themselves are fixed by the tape. questions.topic: The contrastive principle of a concerto grosso
questions.learningObjective: state what opposes what in a concerto grosso
questions.explanation: The small group is the concertino and the large one the ripieno, and the opposition is between them directly: a handful of players alternates with the full body, so the texture swings between exposed lines and a full tutti sonority. questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The original social setting of a sonata
questions.learningObjective: state the social setting the sonata genre began in

questions.topic: A fugue as a genre and as a technique
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a fugue treated as a genre from one used as a technique
questions.explanation: As a genre the fugue is the whole of the piece: an exposition, a development and a cadence, and the music is not doing anything else at any point, so the form is the frame rather than an episode within one. questions.learningObjective: state what a viol's tuning lets its player do and why it is tuned that way
questions.explanation: The tuning lets a player sound a pair of notes as a double stop on a single string, because the intervals between adjacent strings are small enough to be spanned. questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The institutional change a conservatory produced
questions.learningObjective: explain what a conservatory changed about how musicians were trained
questions.explanation: The change is from apprenticeship to standardisation. A graded course makes a specified range of technique the common property of a whole profession, which is what lets an orchestra be assembled from strangers who can all be relied on to read the same notation, and what lets a repertoire be performed as a repertoire rather than as a series of local customs. The cost is that a single method becomes the method, so a player who learned outside it is harder to place, and the practical skills of accompanying and improvising, which were part of the workshop training, are what tend to thin out. The trap is to see only the gain, as though uniformity were free.
questions.hint: Ask what a graded syllabus standardises, and then ask what is lost when a single method becomes the only method.

answer.exemplar: What the institution changed was how a musician is produced, and the change is best described as a move from apprenticeship to standardisation. In a workshop or a church the learner absorbed a craft by doing it alongside a working practitioner, with no syllabus and no examination, so what the pupil got depended on whom the pupil happened to sit with. A conservatory replaces that with a graded course, a fixed body of technique, and a certificate that certifies the same thing wherever it was issued. The musical consequence is direct and large: because a specified range of technique is now the common property of the profession, an orchestra can be assembled from players who have never met, who all read the same notation and can all be relied on to produce a specified sound. That is what makes a shared repertoire performable at all. The cost is equally real. A single method tends to become the only method, so a musician who learned outside it has no obvious place in the profession, and the accompanying and improvising that came with workshop training are the first things to thin out, because they do not fit a scheme of graded exercises. The wrong belief to avoid is that uniformity is free. It buys a profession that can be deployed as a unit, and it pays for that with the narrowing of what counts as a way of playing.

questions.topic: What a recording fixes and what it loses
questions.learningObjective: explain what a recording preserves and what it cannot preserve
questions.explanation: The recording fixes one performance. It preserves the pitches, the timings, the balance and the timbre with a precision no memory can match, and it makes the same playing available repeatedly, which is what turns a repertoire into something a musician can study rather than something that passes. What the live occasion has is the variability: a performance in which the tempo, the dynamics and the phrasing are decided afresh each time, with the players responding to a room, and with the audible risk that makes a good performance a good performance. The recording cannot show that decision having been made, so a listener who only hears records has the result without the act of choosing it.
questions.hint: Ask what the record is of, and what the record cannot show about how the playing was made.

answer.exemplar: A recording and a live performance preserve different things, and the difference is easiest to state as a difference between a result and an act. The recording fixes one performance exactly. It keeps the pitches, the durations, the balance and the timbre with a precision that no memory can match, and that precision is why the recorded performance can be studied: a player can hear how a passage was actually shaped, can hear it again, and can compare two performances of the same music on the same passage. In that sense the record is a genuine gain, because before recording much of what a repertoire consisted of was simply gone once the players who knew it had stopped. What the live occasion has is the variability. Every performance decides its tempo, its dynamics, its balance and its phrasing afresh, in response to a room and to the players listening to each other, and the decision is audible in the result even though it is never audible as such. There is also risk in it, and that risk is part of what a listener values; a performance that could have gone wrong is doing something a record cannot do. So the two are not equivalent. The wrong belief to avoid is the one in the question, that because the recording contains what the players produced it is the same thing. What it contains is a result. The act of choosing the result, which is what a performance is, is left out, and a listener who knows only records has all of the first performance and none of the thing that made it one.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: What the score does in a piece of chance music
questions.learningObjective: explain what the score fixes, what it leaves open and what has been handed over
questions.explanation: The score fixes the frame and releases the content. It fixes the number of events, the range of choices available at each one, the order in which the events happen, and often the timbre and register each choice is drawn from, so the shape and the character of the piece are fully determined in advance. What it leaves open is the actual sequence of outcomes, which is decided during the performance and never the same twice. What the composer has handed over is the selection itself, and that is a real loss of control as well as a release, which is why such pieces are usually short, since there is no predetermined material to unfold.
questions.hint: Ask how many events the score sets out, how wide each choice is, and which of those is settled before anybody plays.

answer.exemplar: A score of this kind fixes everything except the notes. It fixes how many events there are, which here is eight, it fixes the range of choices open at each event, one to six, and it fixes the order in which the events occur together with whatever else the instructions specify about timbre and register. So the length of the piece, its instrumentation, its texture and its general character are all settled in advance and can be relied on. What is not fixed is the outcome: which of the six numbers is chosen at each of the eight events is decided while the piece is being played, and there is no correct sequence, so no performance of the score reproduces another. The composer has therefore handed over the act of selection. That is worth stating precisely, because it is easy to describe such a piece as a framework filled in with anything, and that undersells it: the composer has not abandoned the work but has moved the decision from the desk to the stage, and the decisions then become part of what the audience hears. The cost is that there is no predetermined material to develop, which is why these pieces tend to be brief, since a long span would exhaust a set of choices that is not being replenished. The wrong belief to avoid is that the music is improvised. The score constrains it heavily, and the freedom lies in a narrow and precisely defined choice rather than in an open field.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: How a prepared piano changes the instrument
questions.learningObjective: explain how preparing a piano turns it into a different instrument
questions.explanation: The objects change the instrument's body, not its mechanism. A piano makes its sound in three places at once, the string, the bridge and the soundboard, and the wooden hammers and the resonant structure are what give it the loud singing tone. Putting a weight on a string shortens its speaking length and damps the partials that the bridge and soundboard would otherwise amplify, and felt or rubber takes the attack away, so what is left is the sound of a struck metal object. The instrument is better described as a different one because the change is not a setting, a loudness or a voicing, all of which leave the mechanism producing the same kind of sound, but a replacement of the sound-producing body while the keys and hammers go on working as before.
questions.hint: Ask which parts of the piano produce the sound, and what happens to each when something is placed on a string.

answer.exemplar: The objects change the part of the piano that actually makes the sound. A piano produces its tone in three places at once: the string itself, the bridge that carries the string's motion into the wooden body, and the large resonant soundboard and case that amplify it. The wooden hammers supply a hard attack and the strings and body supply a long ringing resonance, and the two together are what the ear recognises as a piano. Placing a bolt between the strings shortens the length of string that can vibrate and adds its own mass, so the high partials the bridge and soundboard would have amplified are suppressed. Putting felt or rubber against a string removes the attack altogether, so the string is set moving quietly and then decays almost at once, and the bolt and the rubber are struck by the hammer instead. What the ear then hears is a series of small percussive events on metal and rubber, quiet and metallic, and none of the piano's own resonance is left in them. This is why the piano is better described as a different instrument rather than a modified one. A setting, a voicing or a change of loudness leaves the mechanism producing the same kind of sound at a different level, and the sound remains recognisable as a piano in every case. Here the resonating body has been replaced while the keys and hammers go on working exactly as before, so what has been substituted is not a degree of the instrument but its sounding body. The wrong belief to avoid is that preparation is a form of accompaniment or of added percussion. The objects are not played; they are put on the strings so that the piano's own hammers make them speak.
